variants.title: Deploy through both loops
variants.context: A production deployment runs two connected control loops. The serving loop keeps admitted demand inside measured capacity, and the release loop limits how much traffic a candidate receives until production evidence supports more. Every request stays bounded, observable, attributable to a version, and reversible.
variants.prompt: A GenAI assistant is going to production for the first time. Put the deployment stages in order.

items.text: Bound each request: apply authentication, deadlines, context and output limits, admission control, retry budgets, and explicit degraded behavior.
Recover deliberately: route users to the known-good version, preserve traces and decision evidence, and recover mutable state with its own tested plan.
Bound the release: start with shadow or canary traffic, compare the candidate against a stable control, and stop on predeclared gates.
Identify the artifact: pin the application image, model or provider route, prompt, retrieval index, tool contracts, policy, and runtime configuration.

variants.hint: You cannot bound a release whose artifact identity is not pinned.
variants.explanation: The serving loop bounds demand and the release loop bounds exposure, and both depend on a pinned version identity to be reversible.

variants.title: Deploy through both loops
variants.context: A production deployment runs two connected control loops. The serving loop keeps admitted demand inside measured capacity, and the release loop limits how much traffic a candidate receives until production evidence supports more. Every request stays bounded, observable, attributable to a version, and reversible.
variants.prompt: A release changes the system prompt and swaps the retrieval index. Put the deployment stages in order.

items.text: Send shadow or canary traffic and compare candidate answers against the stable control on the predeclared gates.
Enforce the request envelope on the new path: deadlines, context and output limits, retry budget, and tenant quota.
Keep the previous prompt version and index snapshot routable so users can be returned to a known-good path.
Pin the new prompt version and retrieval snapshot alongside the unchanged image digest and model route.

variants.hint: Both the prompt and the index are independently deployable changes.
variants.explanation: Prompt and index are separate versioned artifacts, so each is pinned, exposed gradually, and independently reversible.

variants.title: Deploy through both loops
variants.context: A production deployment runs two connected control loops. The serving loop keeps admitted demand inside measured capacity, and the release loop limits how much traffic a candidate receives until production evidence supports more. Every request stays bounded, observable, attributable to a version, and reversible.
variants.prompt: A candidate release is failing a protected slice at 5 percent traffic. Put the response in order.

items.text: Confirm the request envelope was enforced, so the failure is not overload masquerading as a quality regression.
Route users back to the known-good version and preserve the traces and decision evidence.
Stop the release at the predeclared gate rather than expanding to gather a larger sample.
Recover the mutable state that an application rollback does not restore, using its own tested plan.
Read the release identity on the failing traces: image digest, model route, prompt version, retrieval snapshot, and flag assignment.

variants.hint: One of these steps is not undone by restoring the Pod template.
variants.explanation: Rolling back the application restores the serving path, not schema migrations, prompt aliases, index snapshots, caches, or external side effects.

variants.title: Read the capacity envelope
variants.context: The capacity envelope is read in a fixed order: offered concurrency, ready slots, token demand, the minimum boundary, then bounded overflow. It is a planning envelope, not a latency forecast.
variants.prompt: A team is sizing admission for a new GenAI route. Put the envelope calculation in order.

items.text: Bound overflow by queueing only within an explicit time and depth budget, rejecting or degrading the rest.
Calculate token demand by multiplying request rate by average input-plus-output tokens and by 60 seconds.
Take the minimum boundary, since the safe admission rate is set by whichever capacity saturates first.
Calculate ready slots by multiplying ready replicas by measured concurrency per replica, counting no starting or unready capacity.
Calculate offered concurrency by multiplying arrival rate by measured mean service time.

variants.hint: Work out each boundary separately before comparing them.
variants.explanation: The envelope compares independent boundaries, so the safe admission rate is a minimum rather than a sum or an average.

variants.title: Read the capacity envelope
variants.context: The capacity envelope is read in a fixed order: offered concurrency, ready slots, token demand, the minimum boundary, then bounded overflow. It is a planning envelope, not a latency forecast.
variants.prompt: Replica slots are plentiful but the provider token quota is tight. Put the envelope calculation in order.

items.text: Multiply request rate by average tokens per request and by 60 seconds to get the per-minute token demand.
Take the minimum, which here is the upstream token budget rather than the local slot count.
Multiply ready replicas by concurrency per replica and observe that local slots are not the constraint.
Multiply arrival rate by mean service time to see the active work the traffic implies.
Bound overflow in admission control, because adding replicas cannot raise a provider quota.

variants.hint: Which boundary can autoscaling actually move?
variants.explanation: Token and provider quotas belong in admission control, since scaling Pods adds serving slots but never raises an upstream limit.

variants.title: Read the capacity envelope
variants.context: The capacity envelope is read in a fixed order: offered concurrency, ready slots, token demand, the minimum boundary, then bounded overflow. It is a planning envelope, not a latency forecast.
variants.prompt: A burst arrives while new replicas are still starting. Put the envelope calculation in order.

items.text: Reject or degrade the excess within an explicit queue time and depth budget rather than letting the queue absorb it.
Multiply the burst arrival rate by mean service time to get the offered concurrency.
Multiply only the ready replicas by concurrency per replica, excluding the ones still starting.
Multiply the burst request rate by average tokens per request and by 60 seconds to get token demand.
Take the minimum boundary to find the rate that can actually be admitted during the burst.

variants.hint: Capacity that is not ready yet is not capacity.
variants.explanation: Counting starting replicas inflates the envelope, and an unbounded queue hides overload instead of shedding it.

variants.title: Size the capacity envelope
variants.context: Offered concurrency is arrival rate times mean service time. Ready slots are ready replicas times measured concurrency per replica. Token demand is request rate times average input-plus-output tokens times 60 seconds. The safe admission rate is set by whichever boundary saturates first.
variants.prompt: A deployment has 6 ready replicas and 3 replicas still starting. Load tests show each replica sustains 8 concurrent requests. How many ready slots does the envelope have?
variants.hint: Which replicas are allowed into this number?
variants.explanation: Ready slots are ready replicas times concurrency per replica, so 6 times 8 is 48; starting replicas do not count.

mistakes.feedback: That counts all 9 replicas; starting and unready capacity is excluded from the envelope.
That adds replicas and concurrency instead of multiplying them.

variants.title: Size the capacity envelope
variants.context: Offered concurrency is arrival rate times mean service time. Ready slots are ready replicas times measured concurrency per replica. Token demand is request rate times average input-plus-output tokens times 60 seconds. The safe admission rate is set by whichever boundary saturates first.
variants.prompt: A route serves 40 requests per second and each request averages 1,200 input-plus-output tokens. What is the token demand per minute?
variants.hint: The token boundary is measured over a minute, not a second.
variants.explanation: Token demand is 40 times 1,200 times 60, which is 2,880,000 tokens per minute, or 2.88 million.

mistakes.feedback: That is the per-second figure; the token boundary is expressed per minute, so multiply by 60.
That multiplies by 3,600 seconds, which gives an hourly figure rather than a per-minute one.

variants.title: Size the capacity envelope
variants.context: Offered concurrency is arrival rate times mean service time. Ready slots are ready replicas times measured concurrency per replica. Token demand is request rate times average input-plus-output tokens times 60 seconds. The safe admission rate is set by whichever boundary saturates first.
variants.prompt: Mean service time is 2 seconds, 5 ready replicas each sustain 12 concurrent requests, and the provider allows 1.2 million tokens per minute at an average of 1,000 tokens per request. What is the safe admission rate?
variants.hint: Compute each boundary as a rate, then compare them.
variants.explanation: Slots allow 60 divided by 2, or 30 requests per second, while tokens allow 1,200,000 divided by 60 divided by 1,000, or 20; the minimum is 20.

mistakes.feedback: That is the slot boundary alone; the token budget saturates first and sets the safe rate.
That adds the two boundaries; the envelope takes the minimum, since one saturated resource stops the path.

variants.title: Decide the canary
variants.context: A canary sends a bounded share of representative traffic to a candidate while a stable version stays available as the control and rollback target. Hard boundary violations roll back, incomplete evidence holds, and only a fully passing candidate expands.
variants.prompt: A candidate raises the global task score by 3 points, but a protected enterprise cohort falls below its declared slice tolerance. What is the decision?
options: Expand gradually, because the overall task score improved against the control.
Hold at the current share and keep collecting data on the protected cohort.
Roll back, because a protected slice boundary failed regardless of the global gain.
optionFeedback: Averaging the cohort into the fleet result is exactly how a severe regression gets hidden.
Holding is for incomplete evidence, not for a hard boundary that has already been violated.
Correct: a higher global score never compensates for a failed protected slice or high-impact cohort.
variants.hint: Is this evidence missing, or is it a boundary that already failed?
variants.explanation: Never average away a critical failure: a hard slice, safety, policy, privacy, or correctness violation is a rollback, not a sampling problem.

variants.title: Decide the canary
variants.context: A canary sends a bounded share of representative traffic to a candidate while a stable version stays available as the control and rollback target. Hard boundary violations roll back, incomplete evidence holds, and only a fully passing candidate expands.
variants.prompt: Every declared quality, policy, latency, and efficiency gate passes at 5 percent, the sample meets the minimum, and the stable route is healthy. What is the decision?
options: Promote to 100 percent, since every declared gate has already passed.
Hold at 5 percent until the candidate has run for a full week.
Expand gradually, applying the same abort rules to the next traffic step.
optionFeedback: Passing at 5 percent is evidence about 5 percent; a jump to full traffic removes the bounded blast radius.
An arbitrary wait adds no evidence once the declared sample and gates are already satisfied.
Correct: a fully passing candidate earns the next bounded step, with the same gates still armed.
variants.hint: What does passing at this share entitle the candidate to next?
variants.explanation: Expansion is gradual and each step carries the same abort rules, because evidence gathered at one exposure does not license an unbounded one.

variants.title: Decide the canary
variants.context: A canary sends a bounded share of representative traffic to a candidate while a stable version stays available as the control and rollback target. Hard boundary violations roll back, incomplete evidence holds, and only a fully passing candidate expands.
variants.prompt: All hard boundaries pass, but a collector fault dropped roughly 30 percent of candidate traces during the observation window. What is the decision?
options: Hold expansion until instrumentation is repaired and the window is re-observed.
Expand gradually, since no hard boundary was violated during the window.
Roll back, because missing telemetry means the release cannot be trusted.
optionFeedback: Correct: incomplete instrumentation is a hold, since the gates were evaluated on evidence that is not complete.
Passing gates computed from partial traces do not establish that the boundaries actually held.
Rollback is for a violated boundary; nothing here says the candidate misbehaved.
variants.hint: Separate a failed boundary from evidence you do not actually have.
variants.explanation: Hold when hard boundaries pass but sample size, latency, efficiency, instrumentation, or diagnosis is incomplete.

variants.title: Match the rollout pattern
variants.context: A rollout pattern controls who sees a candidate, how fast exposure grows, and how traffic returns to the stable route. Shadow, canary, blue-green, and rolling update each buy a different thing, and none of them replaces an evidence gate.
variants.prompt: Match each rollout pattern to what it actually provides.

pairs.label: Shadow
pairs.detail: Copies representative inputs to the candidate without using its response, testing integration and performance with no user exposure.

pairs.label: Canary
pairs.detail: Sends a small attributable cohort to the candidate, revealing user outcomes while a flag or router bounds the blast radius.

pairs.label: Blue-green
pairs.detail: Keeps two complete environments and switches traffic between them, making rollback fast at the cost of duplicate capacity.

pairs.label: Rolling update
pairs.detail: Replaces replicas gradually inside one environment, which is efficient but produces mixed-version behavior during the roll.

variants.hint: Ask who sees the candidate's response, and what it costs to take it back.
variants.explanation: The pattern controls exposure and recovery speed; it never substitutes for the predeclared evidence gates.

variants.title: Match the rollout pattern
variants.context: A rollout pattern controls who sees a candidate, how fast exposure grows, and how traffic returns to the stable route. Shadow, canary, blue-green, and rolling update each buy a different thing, and none of them replaces an evidence gate.
variants.prompt: Match each situation to the rollout pattern that fits it.

pairs.label: The team needs latency and integration evidence before any user sees the candidate
pairs.detail: Shadow, because responses are generated but not served.

pairs.label: The team needs real user outcomes from a bounded, attributable cohort
pairs.detail: Canary, because a flag or router keeps the exposed population small.

pairs.label: The team needs the fastest possible traffic switch back to a known-good environment
pairs.detail: Blue-green, because the stable environment stays fully provisioned.

pairs.label: The change is application-compatible and the team wants no duplicate capacity
pairs.detail: Rolling update, because replicas are replaced inside one environment.

variants.hint: Match the requirement to what the pattern buys and what it costs.
variants.explanation: Choosing a pattern is choosing a trade between exposure, evidence, capacity cost, and recovery speed.

variants.title: Match the rollout pattern
variants.context: A rollout pattern controls who sees a candidate, how fast exposure grows, and how traffic returns to the stable route. Shadow, canary, blue-green, and rolling update each buy a different thing, and none of them replaces an evidence gate.
variants.prompt: Match each pattern to the risk it leaves uncovered.

pairs.label: Shadow
pairs.detail: It may not reproduce stateful side effects, so integration health is not the same as production correctness.

pairs.label: Canary
pairs.detail: Small exposure bounds damage but gathers evidence slowly, so gates can stay unresolved for longer.

pairs.label: Blue-green
pairs.detail: State compatibility between the two environments still has to be planned; the switch alone does not migrate data.

pairs.label: Rolling update
pairs.detail: Mixed-version behavior and state changes during the roll need their own explicit tests.

variants.hint: Every pattern buys something and leaves something unmeasured.
variants.explanation: Knowing what a pattern does not cover is what tells you which separate test or state plan the release still needs.
